title: The Rebels Already Won
author: Ken Klippenstein

Wisconsin votes today. If Francesca Hong loses the Democratic gubernatorial
primary, mainstream media will file the story they've been dying to do all
year: that the anti-establishment fever is breaking and the grown-ups are
back.

Don't fall for it. The insurgency already won months ago, before anyone in
Washington even knew who Hong was. It's lame duck hunting season, an electoral
massacre of do-nothing political incumbents and the old ways of politics in
general. Think DOGE, but for politicians. I'll call it DOPE (Department of
Politician Efficiency).

There's the famous examples like Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed, but also
many others. Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old barista, took out 15-term Colorado
congresswoman Diana DeGette, age 69. Darializa Avila Chevalier, a 32-year-old
grad student, did the same to congressman Adriano Espaillat (71), who has held
elected office in upper Manhattan since 1997. Donavan McKinney, a 34-year-old
union organizer, ousted 71-year-old congressman Shri Thanedar in Michigan.

And contrary to the media's lazy comparisons to the Tea Party -- primaries of
which saw defeats of just four House members in 2010 -- the current cycle has
already seen primary defeats of _ten_ House members. That's the most in a non-
redistricting year since 1970, with more primaries yet to come.

But there's more carnage still. A much larger number of politicians ran the
"you can't fire me, I quit" play, rather than face the humiliation of an
election defeat. As a result, sixty-two House members are not seeking
reelection. That's the second-highest number not to seek reelection in
American history.

Also unlike the Tea Party, DOPE is not confined to one political party.
Thirty-five of those House members not seeking reelection are Republicans.
Meanwhile, Marjorie Taylor Greene, who herself chose not to seek reelection,
plans to launch a third-party bid for the presidency, along with recently-
ousted Kentucky congressman Thomas Massie and conservative commentator Tucker
Carlson.

Then there's the survivors who are not long for this world, politically and
often literally given their health issues: people like Senators Mitch
McConnell and Chuck Schumer, members of the crypt caucus.

Being in the middle of all this, I don't think we fully appreciate how
monumental this political realignment is. And DOPE's influence is only
growing.

When Mamdani won the New York mayoral primary, the response from Democratic
"leadership" was awkward silence. Chuck Schumer never endorsed him. Hakeem
Jeffries spent months studying his shoes before finally endorsing, only after
Mamdani had promised to retain police commissioner Jessica Tisch, the national
security schoolmarm who would keep the bucking bronco in line.

Last week though, Democratic officialdom couldn't get in line fast enough
after El-Sayed won the Senate primary in Michigan. Haley Stevens, the
leadership-backed candidate he'd just beaten in a bruising primary, endorsed
him immediately and without any apparent bitterness. Gavin Newsom endorsed him
within minutes of the race being called, then flew to Michigan to campaign
with him. Kamala Harris endorsed him Friday. Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand
put out a joint statement.

These are not backbenchers. Newsom and Harris, both contenders for the next
Democratic Party presidential nomination, evidently concluded that something
so big was transpiring that they were willing to stand next to the guy their
donors just spent millions of dollars trying to bury. None of them asked El-
Sayed to walk anything back, or mentioned his supposed negatives they'd spent
months insisting would prompt the sky to fall.

The party bigwigs clearly see the writing on the wall. It's even changing how
they talk. The most striking example is Biden's former Transportation
Secretary, Pete Buttigieg, who [now
says](https://www.notus.org/2028-election/pete-buttigieg-biden-administration-
interview) his experience in the administration "radicalized" him --
presumably a move to build up populist cred for a presidential run.

Compare that to his 2020 presidential campaign, when Buttigieg couldn't seem
to find an Iowa fairgoer he could resist telling he was a Rhodes Scholar,
speaks six languages (or eight depending on the day), and how much he loves
the James Joyce novel, _Ulysses._ The former McKinsey consultant was the
walking embodiment of why the Democrat Party sucks: over-educated, out of
touch and fixated on wonky, small-bore bullshit lacking any bold vision.

Now he turns up on popular podcasts like _Diary of a CEO_ , where he does some
stupid things -- like pandering to conspiracy heads by
[implying](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mF6uk7UOHBM) that Jeffrey Epstein
compelled Trump to bomb Iran. But he also says things that suggest people's
rage is breaking through.

" Democrats have a responsibility to present something that is better, not
just better than now, but it's gotta be better than before," he told _Diary._

On Democrats fundraising off Trump's collapse: sure, it raises money and it
gets votes, but the trap is that it leaves the party "relieved of having to
generate ideas," Buttigieg [told](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OjAW9kIuLOQ)
Politico recently. In the same interview, he also slammed the party's habit of
acting like we just need to return to some idyllic pre-Trump era, saying:

> "There's a kind of unspoken Democratic assumption that we're trying to take
> us back to, I don't know what. Is it 2012? Is it 1992? Is it 2021? Whatever
> it is, we can't go there. We shouldn't try. We shouldn't want to."

These criticisms of the party are present in virtually all of his recent
interviews, which come off like a repudiation of his own political career.

Sounds to me like DOPE found its way up Mayor Pete's nose. Jokes aside, that's
a good thing. Sincere or not -- and I suspect it's mostly sincere -- it means
the most calibrated politician in the party has read the room and concluded
the old lines don't work anymore.

In other words, pissed off voters won.

A political realignment doesn't get certified on election night. You find out
it happened when you notice the establishment has quietly adopted the
insurgents' vocabulary and ideas -- like Mamdani's "affordability" focus --
and delivers them back to you as conventional wisdom.

This is already happening; the media just hasn't noticed. As with the
Francesca Hong phenomenon, they're too busy fixating on "electability."
There's a word I'd be glad to never hear again.

_Correction:_ An earlier version of this story identified three House
incumbent primary defeats in 2010, but there were four. Article has also been
updated to reflect new incumbent defeats after publication.
